newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australia sorghum gain seen in US corn report.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australia sorghum gain seen in US corn report.

text.p: Lower than expected estimates for 1996 U.S. corn production was encouraging for Australian sorghum, Rob Brealey, trading manager of Queensland grain cooperative Grainco Ltd, said on Monday.
The market had been expecting a 1996 U.S. corn crop of 9.317 billion bushels, ahead of the USDA's final estimate of 9.293 billiion bushels, Brealey said in his weekly market report.
The difference translated to about 600,000 tonnes.
Reduced estimated U.S. sorghum ending stocks would produce a slight tightening in the U.S. supply/demand equation, although production numbers remained large, he said.
Australia's domestic sorghum market remained subdued, with both growers and consumers continuing to stand aside in the short-term, he said.

Sorghum growers were reluctant sellers at current values, while consumers appeared comfortable with the progress of the crop in southern Queensland and were waiting for harvest before taking more coverage, he said.
Central Queensland was enjoying a good start to its sorghum planting, while the northern highlands waited on rain before planting, he said.
In feed barley, values in the recent Saudi Arabian purchase of 1.2 million tonnes were around market expectations of US$155-$161 a tonne, he said.
It was likely that most tonnage would come from Europe, although Canada and the U.S. might also supply, he said.
Some Australian sales were already in place, but it remained to be seen whether more would take place, he said.
Increased export subsidies from the European Union (EU) would increase the likely tonnage from that region, he said.

Australia's domestic feed barley market remained subdued with some grower selling about A$115-A$120 a tonne on farm. Most domestic consumers, however, continued to stand aside from the market in the run-up to the sorghum harvest.

Australia's barley harvest was complete, with estimates of total barley production about six million tonnes (up from 5.5 million tonnes last year), with about 2.5 million tonnes of that malting barley), Brealey said.

The international market, particularly Chinese buyers, appeared to have covered first half 1997 requirements with only spot export business out of Australia to be completed over the next few months, he said.
With new crop EU and Canadian production not available until July/September, the market had support at current export levels of about US$190 a tonne fob Australian ports, he said.
Domestically, malting barley values were steady over the Christmas/New Year break. Grainco's malting barley cash bid finished last week at A$188 a tonne delivered Brisbane.
In cotton, new crop Australian quotes into the Japanese market were being maintained at the US$185-$190 a tonne level for bulk container business into main ports, he said.
Japanese merchants were adopting a wait-and-see atttiutude as production estimates for the Australian crop range from 2.5 million 500 lb bales to 2.8 million bales, he said.
Australia's domestic cottonseed trade was "ticking over" in small parcels, with larger consumers covered reasonably well until new crop became available, he said.
Australia's domestic oilseed values were steady to higher over the past week, with new crop black sunflowers finishing at A$320 a tonne Brisbane and A$315 a tonne Moree for January-April.
-- Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
